In that case, the Kite may capture lighter colored snails preferentially, but supplement with darker snails, therefore appearing to have equal color preference.

Within the Snail Kite population, differences in selection of prey were found between individuals, with some perches containing shell sizes of a broader range as opposed to snails of strictly larger size. The differences may lie between adults and juveniles, with the less experienced juveniles choosing snails of a broader range, making less efficient use of energy.¹ More experienced adults may be more equipped to make the distinction of the energy advantage in larger size snails.¹ During our study, we observed two active perches (Perch 1 and Perch 8) that were occupied by juveniles. These active perches were also shown to have the lowest mean shell sizes, further suggesting these juvenile's inexperience. Another possibility is that the other perches with piles found to contain more variability in shell size came from a breeding Snail Kite couple. A breeding pair will select larger snails to bring back to the nest, while consuming smaller snails themselves and leaving those smaller shells beneath the perch.¹ Since the discarded shells at the perches were collected from both on the surface and below the surface, it is possible that shells were accumulated from different individuals at different points in time. In this case, the snail shell sizes can reveal which individuals may have inhabited a specific perch at one time (for example smaller shells indicate possible presence of juvenile or breeding couple). However, it was observed that all of the active perches with lower mean snail size were inhabited by juveniles.

Another interesting comparison between operculum size and snail size that was conducted reflects a strongly positive relationship between the two. Although the relationship is fairly strong, the lack of a definitive ratio suggests a specific purpose behind these disproportionate characteristics. In one study, it is suggested that this variation is due to a defensive advantage in the shape of the shell.² An odd and unpredictable shape of snail shell will be more difficult for a predator to identify, capture, and consume. In general however, it is thought that freshwater snails have less selective pressure to evolve such elaborate defense mechanisms because there are generally fewer predators in freshwater than in oceans.² However, although the Apple Snails are

freshwater snails, they have many natural predators, including two specialist predators – the Limpkin and Snail Kite.⁷ Therefore, there may be more selectional pressure than usual for a freshwater snail to evolve defensive mechanisms through shell shape and size. Yet another reason for this variability can be revealed through observations made during this study. It was observed throughout the course of the study that many snails had their operculums set farther back into the shell (where the shell is more narrow) while others did not. This would account for the lack of a constant ratio between operculum size and snail shell size, while also suggesting a defensive mechanism. If the operculum is set farther back within the shell, it becomes difficult for the kite to remove the operculum in order to gain access to the snail meat. Therefore, it is beneficial for a snail possessing an extended shell opening. The lack of a direct relationship between operculum size and shell size in this situation cannot be attributed to any one theory with certainty without further investigation.

In order to investigate the presence of any specific plant associations with the Apple Snails, it had to be established that differences existed between the number of live snails collected in each transect. After a Chi Square statistical analysis, it was shown that there were in fact significant differences in the amount collected depending on the location of the transect. Observations of dominant vegetation made in each transect show that transects most abundant in available live snails coincided with the partial or complete dominance of Bladderwort (Utricularia gibba) within the transect. However, it was also determined from these observations that the presence of the Bladderwort was necessary but not sufficient to support a more abundant snail population in a given area (Table 1). Other variables seem to affect the distribution of the snails that were not addressed by the methodology. For example, transects having a thicker layer of floating vegetation generally had a lower abundance of snails. A thicker vegetation layer would limit the amount of oxygen and light available to the snails, so naturally they would avoid these area.¹ Areas with a higher surface temperature also demonstrated a lower abundance than those areas with a more mild surface temperature. In addition, higher snail abundances were found to be in areas of emergent vegetation, especially in areas with higher Thalia geniculata (an emergent aquatic plant) density. Thalia seemed to compose a major egg laying site for Apple Snails at Palo Verde, which may support the fact that a higher abundance of snails were found near areas of higher Thalia density.
